query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The full quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy exhibits superior strain hardening and delayed failure because its higher compositional complexity induces locally heterogeneous lattice distortions and spatial variations in stacking fault energy (SFE), which together promote a more effective interplay between dislocation slip and deformation twinning. In contrast, the quaternary and ternary subsets, although single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing, do not develop the same degree of atomic-scale inhomogeneity, resulting in lower work-hardening rates and earlier failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase FCC microstructure in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets obtained via identical thermomechanical processing.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled room-temperature tensile tests (or equivalent deformation tests) with in situ microstructural imaging (e.g., EBSD and TEM) complemented by atomistic simulations to map local lattice distortions and stacking fault energy distributions.
generation.conditions: Identical thermomechanical processing, single-phase FCC microstructure, room temperature deformation at controlled strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized lattice distortions and spatial heterogeneity in stacking fault energy.
generation.mechanism: The increased number of constituent elements in the quinary alloy creates a rugged energy landscape at the atomic scale. This leads to significant local lattice distortions and a distribution of SFEs that enable a synergistic activation of dislocation slip and deformation twinning, thereby increasing strain hardening and delaying damage accumulation. In contrast, the lower-component alloys lack sufficient complexity to induce the same level of local heterogeneity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical tensile loading, the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy will exhibit a higher work-hardening rate, delayed onset of necking, and an improved balance of strength and ductility relative to the equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets.
generation.baseline: Mechanical behavior (stress–strain response, work-hardening rate, and deformation modes) observed in the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: Applicable for single-phase FCC alloys produced under identical thermomechanical processing conditions and tested under controlled room-temperature tensile (or compressive) deformation conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement in work-hardening or ductility and the relative contributions of lattice distortion versus local SFE variations remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of room-temperature tensile tests on both the full quinary alloy and selected equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets while capturing in situ microstructural evolution using EBSD and TEM. Simultaneously, perform atomistic simulations to quantify local lattice distortions and map the spatial distribution of stacking fault energies. Compare the work-hardening curves, onset of twinning, and microstructural signatures between the alloys.
measurements: Engineering stress–strain curves (with emphasis on work-hardening rates)
In situ EBSD/TEM imaging to examine dislocation arrangements, twin nucleation, and lattice strain distributions
Atomistic simulation outputs quantifying local SFE distributions and lattice distortions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the full quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in work-hardening rate, enhanced deformation twinning, or greater evidence of local lattice distortion and SFE heterogeneity compared to the lower-component subsets under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The stacking fault energy (SFE), which is associated with chemical composition, is one of the most important parameters that influences activated deformation mechanisms, that is, dislocation slip, twinning, and martensitic transformation, during thermomechanical processing and recrystallization []. In low-SFE alloys, dislocations are dissociated into partials, and planar arrays of stacking faults would result in twinning or phase transformation. The improvement on the mechanical properties of Fe40.4Ni11.3Mn34.8Al7.5Cr6 alloy is attributed to the reduction of SFE from 22.2 mJ/m2 to 10.2 mJ/m2, and transition of the slip mode from wavy to planar slip, and micro-band induced plasticity activation []. Reza Razavi et al. suggested the addition of 1.3 wt.% Mo to Fe–33Mn–3Si–2Al twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) steel to reduce the SFE, and increase the ultimate tensile strength and elongation []. Mo acts as a grain boundary stabilizer by forming (Fe, Mo)3C carbides and inhibiting grain coarsening.

In what follows we systematically demonstrate, using an atomistic model that mimics the FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA), the new features rendered by the concentrated compositions: complex stacking fault (CSF) energy (CSFE) that is varying spatially and with processing conditions, local antiphase boundary (APB) energy, unconventional twin boundary energy and martensite phase boundary energy, and elevated lattice resistance to dislocation motion because of the rugged energy landscape. We show that the presence of multi-principal elements and their variable LCO make dislocations behave differently from conventional metals and dilute solutions, in terms of slip paths and activated nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) processes that govern alloy strength. The multitude of (partial) dislocation behavior associated with the adjustable LCOs opens new opportunities to tailor properties, through judicious choice of processing parameters, in particular, the homogenization annealing temperature (Ta).

We manufactured a non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 high-entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC structure. We used in situ neutron diffraction coupled with EBSD and TEM to investigate tensile properties, microstructural evolution, lattice strains, texture development and stacking fault energy. Our main conclusions are drawn as follows: The initial microstructure of the non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 possessed various grain sizes, annealing twins, {111} texture and nano-size chromium carbide. Compared to the equiatomic CoNiCrFe HEA, the non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 HEA manifested a lower electronegativity mismatch, indicating a more stable state of solid solution, which improves its mechanical properties. Compared to the equiatomic CoNiCrFe HEA and other FCC-based non-equiatomic HEAs, the non-equiatomic (CoNi)74.66Cr17Fe8C0.34 HEA revealed a relatively higher tensile strength (770 MPa) and moderate ductility (46%), due to both a stable solid solution and precipitation-strengthened effects. frame.goal: To explain mechanistically why these alloys exhibit different deformation and failure responses compared to the full quinary alloy, beyond what can be accounted for by simple constituent count.
frame.limitation: Using constituent count alone is inadequate to explain the observed variations in mechanical behavior during deformation and failure.

prior_attempts: Prior approaches that correlated mechanical behavior solely with the number of constituent elements have fallen short, implying that factors such as local lattice distortions, variations in stacking fault energies, and potential short-range ordering effects may play a critical role.
